title: FeatCal: Feature Calibration for Post-Merging Models
topic: General Machine Learning->Transfer, Multitask and Meta-learning
claim: Merged models drift away from expert features, especially in later layers; calibration pulls features back and recovers much of the lost accuracy.
layout: 3 panels left-to-right: t-SNE pair, layer-wise line plot, grouped bar chart
description: Three-panel figure with a consistent color code: gray for the merged model (TA), orange for the calibrated model (TA w/ FeatCal), and blue for the expert. Panel (a) shows two t-SNE scatter plots of Stanford Cars final features. In the left plot, TA points (orange-marked as TA) overlap the blue expert cloud only partly. In the right plot, the calibrated points cover the expert distribution more closely. Cosine similarity to the expert is annotated below each plot: 0.60, then 0.84 in bold orange. Panel (b) plots mean L2 distance against layer index 0–11. The gray TA curve climbs steeply in later layers, and the orange calibrated curve stays much lower. Shaded bands show variance. An inset callout reads '46% less drift'. Panel (c) is a grouped bar chart of per-task accuracy over 8 datasets. For each task, the gray TA bar is lowest, the orange calibrated bar is in the middle, and the blue expert bar is highest. The eye goes first to the orange highlights.
caption: Feature drift after Task Arithmetic (TA) merging and \method calibration in CLIP-ViT-B/32. Panels (a,b) use Stanford Cars: \method moves features toward expert features, raises their mean cosine similarity from 0.60 to 0.84, and reduces mean L2 feature drift, with 46% less final-layer drift. Panel (c) reports per-task accuracy in the 8-task setting. [ref] gives full 8-task feature views.
abstract: Model merging combines task experts into one model and avoids joint training, retraining, or deploying many expert models, but the merged model often still underperforms task experts. We study this performance gap through feature drift, the difference between features produced by the merged model and by the expert on the same input. Our theory decomposes this drift into upstream propagation and local mismatch, tracks how it propagates and combines through later layers in forward order, and links final feature drift to output drift. This view motivates FeatCal, which uses a small calibration set to calibrate the merged model weights layer by layer in forward order, reducing feature drift while staying close to merged weights and preserving the benefits of model merging. FeatCal uses an efficient closed-form solution to update model weights, with no gradient descent, iterative optimization, or extra modules. On the main CLIP and GLUE benchmarks, FeatCal beats Surgery and ProbSurgery, the closest post-merging calibration baselines: 85.5% vs. 77.0%/78.8% on CLIP-ViT-B/32 Task Arithmetic (TA) and 85.2% vs. 83.7%/82.2% on FLAN-T5-base GLUE. On CLIP-ViT-B/32, 8 examples per task reach 82.9%, and 256 examples per task take 53 seconds, about 4x faster than both baselines, showing better sample efficiency and lower calibration cost.
